tmott13 / bookmark-buddy

🦥 Tidies your messy bookmarks with Gemma running on your device, then sorts new ones as you save them. A Chrome/Edge extension plus a web app. Nothing is uploaded, and you can undo everything.

🦥 Bookmark Buddy

Your messy bookmarks, tidied while you put your feet up. Meet Mochi, the sloth who does the tidying 🦥🍡

Bookmark Buddy sorts your bookmarks into clean folders, catches duplicates, and keeps everything tidy as you save new ones. The sorting is done by Gemma running in your browser with WebLLM, so your bookmarks (your bank, your job search, your health sites…) never leave your device.

It comes two ways:

  • 🧩 Chrome / Edge extension (the lazy way): tidies your real bookmarks in place, with one-click Undo everything, then sorts new bookmarks automatically as you save them.
  • 🌐 Web app: bookmark-buddy.onrender.com. Works in any WebGPU browser. Drop in a bookmarks export and download a tidy file to import back.

Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 3: Slow and Steady.

Install the extension

  1. Download bookmark-buddy-extension.zip from the latest release and unzip it.
  2. Go…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

  • Open model: Gemma 2 2B (gemma-2-2b-it-q4f16_1-MLC) on laptops, with Gemma 3 1B as the lighter option for phones.
  • Runs in the browser: WebLLM runs Gemma on your GPU with WebGPU. The model downloads once and is cached, so it even works offline.
  • Frontend: Angular 22 with signals. Your session is saved in your browser, so a refresh doesn't lose your progress.
  • Extension: Manifest V3. The same Angular app is the extension's page. A small background worker listens for new bookmarks, and when one needs a folder it opens a hidden offscreen page that runs Gemma on the GPU, then closes it a few minutes later to give the memory back.
  • Hosting: a free static site on Render, with no backend at all.

Like my last two projects, the big idea is Gemma makes the judgment calls, and the app keeps your data safe:

  1. Gemma never touches a URL. It only sees each bookmark's title and website, and replies with a folder name. The app copies the actual links, dates and icons, so nothing can get mangled.
  2. Nothing gets deleted unless you say so. Duplicates and old dev links go into a "Maybe delete?" folder with a reason, so you decide. You can delete anything with one click (or clear out the whole "Maybe delete?" folder), and restore it until you apply. The extension saves a backup first and can undo everything.
  3. Nothing gets lost. If Gemma skips a bookmark or makes up a folder name, the app catches it and puts it in "Other." Every bookmark you keep ends up in a folder.
  4. Small batches, with examples. A 2B model does much better sorting 6 bookmarks than 300, so it works through them in small batches, slow and steady, like a sloth. Each batch also shows Gemma a few bookmarks it already sorted, so similar pages land in the same folder.
  5. The app handles the obvious ones. If a title or site clearly names a folder ("Easy taco recipe" → Recipes), the app files it without asking Gemma. Gemma only gets the judgment calls.
  6. It learns as it goes. Once Gemma puts the same site in the same folder twice, the rest of that site's bookmarks follow automatically, which saves time. Sites with every kind of content, like YouTube and Reddit, always get a fresh look. When you save a bookmark into a folder yourself, or hit Undo on a guess, Mochi learns from that too.
  7. It never blocks you. If Gemma isn't downloaded yet, a new bookmark waits in a "Needs a home" folder until you open Bookmark Buddy, instead of getting lost.

I was surprised by how well Gemma worked to generate the proper folder names for my bookmarks. I also loved how fast Mochi worked to organize all of my bookmarks.

My first version didn’t get it right. Gemma sorted 12 bookmarks at a time, and my recipes ended up scattered across a few different folders. The fix was slowing it down: 6 bookmarks at a time, plus a few already-sorted examples so Gemma stays consistent. Turns out slow and steady really does win, just like Mochi.

I built this with Claude as my pair programmer. I picked the problem, made the product calls, and tested it on my own bookmarks.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • Bookmarks are personal. They show your bank, your job search, your health sites, your hobbies. With an open model running on your own device, none of that gets uploaded to anyone's server.
  • It's free to run. No API bill, no subscription. Set it up once, tidy whenever you want.
  • It works offline. Once Gemma is downloaded, you can tidy your bookmarks on a plane.
  • I control the whole pipeline. I decide what the model sees (titles, not URLs), how it's batched, and the safety rules around it. A closed API would be a black box in the middle of my bookmarks.

The Lazy Payoff

I was able to organize all 722 of my bookmarks! I also kept my folders, which I loved.

It took me about 15 minutes in total to organize my bookmarks. I had about 40 bookmarks that Mochi put into an "Other" folder that I went through line by line to sort. The app did everything I needed it to do. I love that I could drag n drop bookmarks, create new folders, and delete bookmarks, all in one place! This app saved me so much time and it was very low effort. Perfect for a lazy sloth like myself.

What's Next: Bookmark Buddy 1.1.0

  • Chrome Web Store and Edge Add-ons: a one-click install with automatic updates, no Developer mode needed
  • Right-click "Ask Mochi to file this": sort any bookmark on demand, including old ones sitting in the wrong folder
  • A weekly tidy-up: a gentle nudge like "Mochi found 4 bookmarks that could use a home," then one click to review
  • A toolbar popup: see what's waiting in "Needs a home" and turn auto-sorting on or off without opening a full tab
  • A first-run welcome: a quick tour of what Mochi does and help picking a Gemma model

What should Mochi learn next? Tell me in the comments 🦥

Prize Categories

  • Gemma: Gemma 2 2B and Gemma 3 1B run fully in the browser with WebLLM, suggesting folders, sorting every bookmark, and filing new ones in the background.
  • Render: the web version is deployed as a free Render static site from a render.yaml blueprint.

Thanks to DEV, the Hacktoberfest team, and the MLC/WebLLM and Gemma teams. And a belated Happy International Sloth Day (Oct 20) from Mochi! 🦥

articles.title: My Reducer's Switch Stopped Being Exhaustive. `as const` Fixed It.
articles.description: Object and array literals widen to `string` and `number` the moment you write them, which quietly breaks discriminated unions and exhaustive switch checks. `as const` keeps the literal types — but it also freezes the value, which bites in its own way.
articles.body_html:
The PR review catches it at the worst possible moment — the day after it shipped. A teammate added a 'reset' action to the cart reducer, ran the tests, watched them pass, and merged. The switch statement never ran the new branch. Not an error. Not a warning. The build was green the whole time.

Here's the reducer, trimmed down to the shape that matters:

function cartReducer(state: CartState, action: { type: string; payload?: unknown }) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'add':
      return { ...state, items: [...state.items, action.payload] };
    case 'remove':
      return { ...state, items: state.items.filter((i) => i.id !== action.payload) };
    // 'reset' was added here as an afterthought, then deleted by accident
    // during a rebase. TypeScript never noticed either way.
  }
  return state;
}

action.type is typed as string. TypeScript can check a switch against a union of specific values and tell you when a case is missing. It cannot check a switch against all possible strings — there's no way to be "exhaustive" over an infinite type. So the compiler does the only honest thing: it says nothing.

The bug wasn't the missing case. The bug was string — and it was there before anyone touched the reducer.

Where the type actually came from

Nobody typed action.type: string on purpose. It came from the action creators:

function reset() {
  return { type: 'reset' };
}

reset(); // return type: { type: string }

That's the part that surprises people. reset is a const-worthy, never-reassigned function returning a single literal. You'd expect { type: 'reset' } to stay exactly that specific. It doesn't — and the reason is really about mutability, not constants.

const status = 'idle';
// type: 'idle' — status can never change, so TypeScript keeps the literal

const config = { status: 'idle' };
// config.status type: string — config.status CAN be reassigned
// (config.status = 'loading' compiles fine), so TypeScript widens
// the property to the general type that covers anything you might assign

A const binding to a primitive can't be reassigned, so TypeScript has no reason to generalize — the literal type is the only thing it will ever hold. A property inside an object is a different story: config is const, but config.status isn't. TypeScript widens object and array members to their general type — string, number, boolean — because it's inferring a type that has to tolerate future writes, not just describe the value in front of it. Same rule for arrays:

const methods = ['GET', 'POST'];
// type: string[] — any string could get pushed in later

That widening is usually what you want. It's only a problem when the whole point of the value was to be one of a fixed, known set — an action's type, a theme name, an HTTP method you're about to switch on.

Before you scroll — what do you think turns string back into the literal 'idle'?

as const tells TypeScript to stop generalizing

as const is a type assertion that does the opposite of widening: it takes the literal, narrowest type of exactly what you wrote, and makes every property (recursively) readonly so there's no future write to protect against.

const config = { status: 'idle' } as const;
// config.status type: 'idle'  (readonly)

const methods = ['GET', 'POST'] as const;
// type: readonly ['GET', 'POST']  — a fixed-length, literal tuple, not string[]

Apply it to the action creators and the whole chain fixes itself:

function reset() {
  return { type: 'reset' } as const;
}
function add(payload: Item) {
  return { type: 'add', payload } as const;
}
function remove(id: string) {
  return { type: 'remove', payload: id } as const;
}

type CartAction = ReturnType<typeof reset> | ReturnType<typeof add> | ReturnType<typeof remove>;
// { type: 'reset' } | { type: 'add'; payload: Item } | { type: 'remove'; payload: string }

action.type inside the reducer is now 'add' | 'remove' | 'reset' instead of string — a real, finite union. Switch over it, and TypeScript can finally do the one thing it couldn't before:

function cartReducer(state: CartState, action: CartAction): CartState {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'add':
      return { ...state, items: [...state.items, action.payload] };
    case 'remove':
      return { ...state, items: state.items.filter((i) => i.id !== action.payload) };
    default:
      return assertNever(action); // ← now a compile error if a case is missing
  }
}

function assertNever(x: never): never {
  throw new Error(`Unhandled action: ${JSON.stringify(x)}`);
}

Delete the 'reset' case and action reaching the default branch is no longer never — it's { type: 'reset' }, which doesn't satisfy assertNever's never parameter. TypeScript flags it at the call site, at compile time, before a reviewer has to catch it by reading carefully. That's the whole fix: one three-letter suffix, in the three functions that build the actions.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The part that bites back

Here's where it gets uglier, and where most explanations of as const stop too early. as const didn't just lock in the literal type — it made the value readonly, all the way down. That's not a side effect you can opt out of; it's the mechanism.

const METHODS = ['GET', 'POST'] as const;

METHODS.push('PUT');
// Error: Property 'push' does not exist on type 'readonly ["GET", "POST"]'

A readonly tuple has no mutating methods at all — no push, pop, splice, or index assignment. That's usually fine; you reached for as const because you wanted a fixed set, not a growable list. But it surfaces somewhere you won't expect the first time:

function logAllowedMethods(methods: string[]) {
  console.log(methods.join(', '));
}

logAllowedMethods(METHODS);
// Error: Argument of type 'readonly ["GET", "POST"]' is not assignable
// to parameter of type 'string[]'. The type 'readonly ["GET", "POST"]'
// is 'readonly' and cannot be assigned to the mutable type 'string[]'.

logAllowedMethods never mutates its argument, but its signature promises TypeScript it's allowed to. TypeScript can't verify that promise against a value it knows is frozen, so it refuses the call outright — correctly, because somewhere else methods.push(...) really would be legal against that same signature. Two ways out, and they mean different things:

function logAllowedMethods(methods: readonly string[]) { /* ... */ }
logAllowedMethods(METHODS); // fine — the parameter now admits it won't mutate

// or, if the function genuinely can't change:
logAllowedMethods([...METHODS]); // fine — a fresh, mutable copy

Widen the parameter if the function is well-behaved and just reads. Copy the array if you don't control the function. Either is one line; the trap is not knowing which bug you're looking at when the red squiggle shows up two files away from the as const that caused it.

Where it's worth reaching for

  • Action/event objects — reducers, event buses, anywhere a type or kind field drives a switch. This is the highest-leverage use; it's the difference between a real exhaustiveness check and a decorative one.
  • Fixed option lists — const THEMES = ['light', 'dark', 'system'] as const; then type Theme = (typeof THEMES)[number]; gives you the union 'light' | 'dark' | 'system' for free, generated from the one array you'll actually iterate to build a <select>.
  • Enum-free constant maps — const Role = { ADMIN: 'admin', EDITOR: 'editor' } as const; reads better than a TypeScript enum for most teams and gives you (typeof Role)[keyof typeof Role] as the type.
  • Not for values you're going to mutate. If you need to .push() into it later, as const is actively the wrong tool — reach for an explicit type annotation instead.

And if you're already validating the shape against an interface, you may not need as const at all — satisfies checks a value against a type and keeps its inferred literals, in one step, without the readonly. The two solve overlapping problems from opposite directions: as const narrows by removing information you didn't ask TypeScript to track (mutability); satisfies narrows by not throwing away information you already had. Worth knowing both before reaching for either.

The missing 'reset' case made it to production because string doesn't have gaps to find. as const is how you tell TypeScript the value in front of it is the only value it will ever be — so when you miss one, the compiler misses it too, loudly, before a reviewer has to.

Where has a widened type let a real bug through for you — and did you reach for as const, or something else?

articles.title: Trailing Slash SEO: Stop the Redirect Loop Before Choosing a URL Style
articles.description: When a trailing-slash redirect loops, trace the rules that add and remove the slash before choosing a...
articles.body_html:
When a trailing-slash redirect loops, trace the rules that add and remove the slash before choosing a preferred URL style. An edge rule can send a request toward the slash version while the application sends it back. A canonical tag inside the intended page cannot make that page reachable through a repeating redirect.

For SEO, the first useful result is a request that reaches the correct public answer and stops. After that, align the redirect policy, internal links and other URL signals. Changing a slash convention alone does not establish better rankings or a future AI citation.

The example below is a hypothetical diagnostic exercise. No production service was tested or changed for this article. The aim is to separate three problems that often get combined in a URL audit: two successful duplicate pages, an unnecessary chain and a loop that never reaches the content.

Separate the path from the root address

Google's trailing-slash explanation distinguishes paths such as https://example.com/topic and https://example.com/topic/ as separate URLs. It does not give one style an inherent search advantage. The bare origin, https://example.com, is equivalent to https://example.com/; do not treat that root case as evidence about every path.

Write down the path pair you actually need to investigate. Preserve the hostname, scheme and relevant query parameters in the record. If those change as well, describe each change rather than assigning every hop to a slash rule.

Confirm that the two paths are intended to represent the same answer before consolidating them. A shared visual design does not prove equivalent content. A documentation route, a file download and an application action may have different behavior even when their addresses look related. Keep the investigation tied to the specific public content route.

Record each hop before following the whole chain

Inspect the response for the exact input URL. Record the status and any redirect destination, then inspect that destination in turn. Use the team's normal request-inspection tools and preserve the observed sequence. A browser's final address can hide intermediate hops when the navigation eventually succeeds.

For a repeating sequence, identify the first URL that reappears. That gives the team a bounded loop to investigate. Do not keep following it indefinitely, and do not summarize the problem as a slow page when the request never reaches the document.

Keep the public request path separate from an internal rewrite. A rewrite may change how a server finds content without telling the client to navigate to another URL. Diagnose the externally observed status and destination first, then use the configuration owners' evidence to explain which layer produced them. Do not infer that ownership from a status code alone.

Trace a fictional edge and application conflict

Suppose a fictional documentation site receives a request for https://example.com/docs/topic. Its edge rule redirects to https://example.com/docs/topic/. The application then redirects that slash version back to https://example.com/docs/topic. The original input appears again, so another pass repeats the same conflict.

This trace contains two incompatible decisions about the preferred form. It does not show that either form is universally wrong. The useful repair is to agree on the intended destination for this route and make the layers compatible with that decision.

In a real incident, attach the observed response sequence and the relevant configuration evidence to the handoff. The edge and application owners should be able to recognize their respective rules. Do not label the example as a real CDN defect, claim a particular framework caused it or copy a blanket redirect rule into production without reviewing the site's route behavior.

Classify duplicate pages, extra hops and loops differently

If both route versions return successful content, compare the content and intended purpose. That is a duplication or route-policy question. It is different from a loop because a person or crawler can reach a document through each route.

If one version redirects through an intermediate URL before reaching the right content, record the chain. The destination is reachable, but the routing may be doing unnecessary work. Investigate whether related host, scheme and path rules can agree on a direct destination without changing the route's meaning.

If the sequence repeats, prioritize restoring a stable endpoint. Adding a canonical tag, resubmitting a sitemap or rewriting the article's opening would not resolve the conflicting HTTP responses. Google's redirect guidance explains how redirects communicate a destination and how permanent redirects act as a canonicalization signal. Apply that guidance to the intended move, not as a substitute for diagnosis.

Test both inputs and the intended final document

The first test case starts with the non-slash path. Record the expected destination and compare it with the actual hops. The second starts with the slash path. A repair is incomplete if one input succeeds while the other still cycles.

The third case requests the intended final URL directly. It should serve the expected public answer under the tested conditions, rather than sending the request back into another normalization step. Verify the document's identity as well as its successful status; reaching an unrelated page is not a correct route repair.

For each case, record the input, observed responses, final document, date and relevant environment. These are diagnostic records, not a ranking test. A successful request proves a narrower result than indexing or appearance in search. Keep later discovery checks separate from the immediate routing verification.

Check query strings and file paths without applying a blanket rule

A fourth case can use a meaningful query parameter on the content route. Decide what that parameter does before evaluating the redirect. Dropping a required language or version selection could change the answer even if the resulting URL looks cleaner.

A fifth case should cover a relevant file or endpoint near the affected route pattern. For example, a downloadable document may need different handling from a directory-like page. The goal is to catch an overly broad rule, not to require every address on the site to follow one cosmetic shape.

Add cases for the site's actual exceptions when the routing owners identify them. Keep this review focused on public content behavior and established expectations. Do not change authentication, form submissions or API requests as an incidental part of an SEO cleanup. Those routes need their own tested requirements and responsible review.

Align the places that publish the preferred URL

Once the endpoint is stable, inspect the links and metadata for the affected page. Internal links, sitemap entries and any canonical declaration should identify the intended version consistently. Update the actual sources that generate these values rather than manually correcting one rendered page while leaving the template unchanged.

Compare the chosen canonical with the document it describes. A routing fix should not leave the page declaring a different language, version or product as its preferred representative. The question is whether the signals identify the correct answer, not whether every URL now has a matching final character.

Use a permanent redirect when that accurately represents the route policy and the alternate address should lead to the preferred equivalent. Preserve a clear rollback plan for the routing change through the site's normal release process. This article describes the checks; it does not establish that a change has been deployed or verified on your system.

Close the routing incident before claiming a discovery win

After the responsible team applies a repair, repeat the same request cases and compare the observed paths. Keep evidence that the loop stopped and the intended document is reachable. Check for a cached old response if the public behavior differs from the expected current configuration, using the team's normal diagnostic process.

Then monitor the relevant search records separately. A reachable page may still face indexing, relevance or other discovery questions. An AI answer may cite a different source even when the route is healthy. Do not turn a successful HTTP check into a promised increase in mentions or recommendations.

Choose one affected public answer and follow its two route variants from input to final document. If the paths disagree, resolve the layer conflict first. A consistent final URL is useful because readers can reach the answer they requested, whatever slash convention the site adopts.

This is my submission for Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady.
PRESENTING ~~ [www.studysloth.tech]

Study Sloth: for the student with 8 units, 4 lab records and 1 night left

It's 11:47 PM. Your exam is at 9 AM.
You have a 90-minute lecture recording you never rewatched, a PDF called unit3_FINAL_final2.pdf, a lab record due in the morning, and a group chat full of people asking "does anyone have notes?"

If that made your stomach drop a little, this post is for you. I built Study Sloth because I've been that student.

Sound familiar?

1. The 90-minute recording you will never rewatch.
You were in the lecture. You still don't know what was taught. The recording sits in a folder, quietly judging you.

2. Your material lives in six places.
Board photos in the gallery, PDFs named unit3_FINAL_final2.pdf, half-written notes in a chat with yourself. And at 1 AM, 40 people ask the group: "does anyone have the Unit 3 notes?"

3. The notes that cost me marks.
I once leaned on last-minute AI notes. They were correct, but they weren't what my teacher had taught, so I lost marks for things that weren't wrong, just never taught. (I was too smart to pay attention in class. Lesson learned, painfully.)

4. Flashcards that take longer to make than to study.
You spend the whole evening formatting cards, then have no time left to learn a single one.

5. The lab record. Again. And then the viva.
The same template every time: rewrite the aim, theory, procedure and conclusion, paste the code and output, fight the formatting. Then the examiner asks, "Why did you use a LEFT JOIN here?" About your own code. "Because it worked" is not an answer.

Five problems. One night. Zero chill.

So I built the buddy I wanted

I went looking for a tool that did all this. Umm, I couldn't find one. So, as the wise developers once said:

BUILD IT.

...and that's exactly what I did.

Study Sloth is a study workspace that does the setup work, so you can get to the learning sooner. It doesn't learn for you. It turns what you already have into what you need.

Here's how it answers each of those:

The pain What Study Sloth does
The recording you won't rewatch Turns it into a timestamped transcript and notes by unit
Material in six places One subject folder per course: syllabus, lectures, PDFs, labs and cards, with PDFs turned into notes with page references
Notes that weren't what was taught Works from your lectures and your PDFs, and every point carries a timestamp or page number so you can check it
Flashcard-making Generates flashcards, quizzes and likely viva questions in the same step
The lab record and the viva Builds a lab manual from your experiment titles, using your real outputs when you have them. Its questions flow into the Study Deck, so you can practise "why did I do this?"

It's also the one-night-before-exams buddy for people who work best under pressure (hi, it's me). Just don't make it your only plan.

What I Built

  • Organise a course: turn a syllabus into units and topics.
  • Study from PDFs: upload a text-based PDF and get structured notes with page references.
  • Review lectures: turn audio or video into a timestamped transcript, then notes by unit.
  • Practise actively: flashcards, quizzes, and likely viva questions.
  • Prepare lab records: build a manual from your experiment titles. Use your real outputs when you have them. When you don't, the manual can include generated expected outputs, labelled as expected, not yours.
  • Keep revision connected: lab-manual flashcards and quizzes appear in the same Study Deck.

There are three ways to use it, and they handle your data differently:

Version What it does Where your data goes
Local app Everything: lectures, PDFs, labs, study deck Stays on your computer (local Ollama and Whisper)
Hosted workspace (Render) The full interface in a browser Text goes to [model provider]; recordings go to Groq for transcription; data is temporary
Lightweight notes page PDF or pasted text in, study set out Text goes to [model provider]; nothing is stored

Demo

  • Live: - [studysloth.tech]/[www.studysloth.tech]
  • Code: The source is available here:

AaliyaKhan25 / Study-Sloth

Hacktober Fest 2k26

Study Sloth

Turn study material into a study plan you can actually use.

Study Sloth is an AI-assisted study workspace that transforms notes, syllabi, lectures, and lab work into organized learning materials—so students can spend less time formatting and more time understanding.

Features · Get started · AI models · Deployment · Contributing


Why Study Sloth?

Studying often means jumping between lecture files, notes, flashcards, quizzes, code, and lab-record templates. Study Sloth brings those tasks together in one calm, student-focused interface. Add your material and build a useful next step from it: clearer notes, revision questions, or a structured lab record.

The project has three ways to use it:


























Experience Best for Entry point
Local Study Sloth A personal workspace, including video/audio lecture transcription and lab tools app.main:app
Hosted Study Sloth A browser-based workspace hosted on Render web:app
Study Sloth Online A lightweight notes-and-PDF study-material generator online:app

The hosted and…


View on GitHub


Also, do check out my GitHub Profile: [https://github.com/AaliyaKhan25]

A note on the live version: on Render's free tier, the filesystem is temporary, so workspaces and uploads can disappear after a restart. It's a demo, not a vault.

How I Built It

Python, FastAPI, SQLite, and plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Slow work (transcription, long PDFs) runs as background jobs, so the browser shows progress instead of waiting on one long request.

  • Study material: Gemma 4:cloud and Gemma3:4b , through an Ollama-compatible API. The text model and the vision model are separate settings, so either can be swapped by changing one value.
  • Transcription: locally, faster-whisper on the GPU. Hosted, Groq's whisper-large-v3-turbo, because running Whisper on a small Render plan wasn't practical. The trade-off: recordings are sent to Groq, uploads are limited to 25 MB, and quotas may apply.
  • Checkable notes: every point keeps its timestamp or page number.
  • Lab records: you can enter your own outputs, and you confirm and review the record before printing.

What Went Wrong (and What I Learned)

1. "New" doesn't mean "compatible." Video uploads failed with TypeError: open() got an unexpected keyword argument 'metadata_errors', even though PyAV was already very recent. Reproducing the exact call showed the installed PyAV rejected the keyword; faster-whisper passed. I pinned a compatible range, added a regression test, and added a CPU fallback for when CUDA is detected, but its libraries are missing. "Upgrade everything" wasn't the fix.

2. The cloud changes what "local" means. Once the app was hosted, labels like "stays on this computer" became untrue, and file paths broke. One Render deploy built fine and then crashed at startup because /var/data wasn't a mounted disk. The app now falls back to temporary storage with a warning, and the hosted page rewrites its labels to say what really happens to your data.

3. Keep visitors' workspaces apart. Hosted visitors get a cookie-based workspace. Python's contextvars don't follow work into worker threads, so I copy the request context into each job. This isn't an account system: there's no sign-in, so treat a workspace as private-ish, not a secure vault.

4. Failures should be loud. An early version swallowed model errors, so a broken job looked like an empty result. Now a failed job shows its real error in the app. The tests cover the awkward paths too: transcription fallback, Groq response handling, a missing disk path, and manually linked cards. All 9 pass locally, which proves those code paths, not that the public deployment is live.

How I Used GitHub Copilot

I used GitHub Copilot in VS Code while building and debugging, for example, on the PyAV problem, the hosted-service behaviour, tests, and docs. GitHub Actions also ran the tests on every push. Copilot helped build the app; Gemma is the model inside it. They do different jobs.

Why Open Innovation Matters

Studying shouldn't depend on one closed assistant that you can't inspect, can't run offline, and can't afford when the free plan runs out. Open models let me choose the tool for the job and the hardware. Because the model is just a setting, I could run Gemma locally for privacy and still point the hosted version at a different provider.

That also means "open" doesn't mean "everything on one server". Gemma writes the study material and Groq handles hosted transcription, so users should know which service sees what. Being honest about that trade-off is part of building with open tools.

The Lazy Payoff

I won't invent a "minutes saved" number. [Time one real lecture or PDF and add it: "A 10-minute lecture became unit-wise notes, 8 flashcards and 5 quiz questions in X minutes."]. The aim is fewer blank-page moments: source material in, a first draft of notes and practice out.

If you try it, tell me which pain point it fixed for you, and which one it still doesn't.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 3 4B is the default model for study material.
  • Best Use of a .tech Domain: [www.studysloth.tech]. It's my first domain, and a .tech one. Thank you, Hacktoberfest and MLH!
  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot: - Lifesaver for me; helped me resolve a hell lot of bugs. TYSM GitHub Copilot
  • Best Use of Render: - My deployment buddy for life , not just Hacktober; Render has always been there

Study smarter. Stay curious. Let the Sloth handle the busywork.

articles.description: If robots.txt returns a 503 error, restore delivery of the intended crawl rules before rewriting your...
articles.body_html:
If robots.txt returns a 503 error, restore delivery of the intended crawl rules before rewriting your product pages. A working homepage does not show that Google can retrieve the rules for that host. Treat the rules endpoint and the content endpoints as separate checks, then verify crawl activity after the delivery problem is fixed.

This is a specific technical discovery problem. It can interrupt the route to Google Search even when the page itself looks healthy. It does not prove why a brand is missing from ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, and the behavior described here should not be applied to every crawler.

The incident below is hypothetical. It shows how to organize an investigation without claiming that a real site was tested or that repairing one response guarantees indexing, rankings or AI citations.

Distinguish an unavailable rule file from a blocking rule

A 503 response and an intentional Disallow directive describe different conditions. One says the server could not deliver a resource. The other is a rule inside a delivered file. Editing the text of a file is unlikely to solve a request that never reaches that file.

Google's robots.txt specification describes an initial 12-hour crawl pause after server errors, with continued attempts to fetch the file. Later behavior depends on cached rules, elapsed time and site availability. Read the documented sequence rather than treating a 503 as an immediate permanent removal.

Start the incident record with the observed response, not an assumed policy. Write “the rules request returned 503 at this time” instead of “Google is blocked.” The narrower statement gives engineering a condition it can reproduce and avoids confusing delivery failure with an editorial or indexing decision.

Check the exact public host and request

Record the complete robots.txt URL, including protocol and hostname. The rules for the marketing host and the documentation host may be separate. A successful check on one is not a substitute for checking the other. Include any port that is part of the public address.

Use a normal GET request to inspect the status and returned content. Record redirects, response headers, the final URL and a short description of the body. A status-only probe can miss an application error page that was returned with an apparently successful status.

Keep the record small enough to compare across checks. Useful fields include time, host, request method, observed status, response type, relevant cache information and the intended rules version. Do not put credentials, private cookies or unrelated request data into a public incident write-up.

Trace the layer that produced the response

Compare the response at the public edge with what the origin would return through your approved diagnostic process. The edge is the layer users and crawlers normally reach first, such as a content delivery network or gateway. The origin is the service behind it.

If the origin serves the intended file while the public endpoint returns an error, inspect the route between them. Look for a failed deployment, a route accidentally handled by the application, an unavailable dependency or a cached error. These are investigation candidates, not a diagnosis established by the mismatch alone.

If both layers fail, follow the request through the service that owns the resource. Assign the endpoint an owner. A small text file can become an unowned dependency when marketing assumes infrastructure serves it and infrastructure assumes the web application does.

Work through a bounded incident example

Imagine a fictional SaaS site with a marketing homepage and public documentation on the same host. After a release, the homepage returns its normal content, but the robots.txt request returns a 503 page generated by a gateway. The team first notices fewer crawler requests in its logs.

The tempting response is to change the documentation headings or remove restrictions from the file. Neither follows from the evidence yet. The initial question is whether the deployed route can deliver the approved rules. The team compares the current route configuration with the last working deployment and checks whether the file depends on the failing application service.

Suppose, within this example, the route was unintentionally changed to forward the request through that service. Restoring the intended delivery path addresses the observed failure. It does not establish that every later traffic change came from this incident. The example ends with a verifiable request result, not an invented ranking recovery.

Preserve the policy while restoring delivery

Use the approved file as the reference for the repair. Check the expected groups, paths and sitemap entries against the intended version. Avoid replacing the file with an empty response simply because that removes the immediate server error. Availability and policy correctness are separate requirements.

Review the change with whoever owns crawler policy. A technical incident should not quietly expand what can be crawled. Equally, a broad temporary restriction should not become permanent because nobody schedules its review. Record both the operational repair and any deliberate policy change as distinct decisions.

Google's documentation also distinguishes most 4xx responses from server errors. Do not manufacture a 404 or 403 as a shortcut around a broken delivery path. Choose the response that accurately represents the intended resource and verify the relevant provider's interpretation before changing its status behavior.

Use two recovery gates

The first gate is delivery recovery. Repeated checks should reach the correct endpoint and receive the intended rules, without the earlier error or an unexpected application page. Check the affected public host and relevant edge locations available through your normal monitoring. Save enough evidence to identify the deployed version.

The second gate is observed crawler recovery. Check fresh request logs and Google's Crawl Stats report for the affected property. That report includes host availability information and crawl responses. Its reporting window is different from a direct request made now, so compare timestamps before describing a mismatch as a new failure.

Passing the first gate does not automatically pass the second. Nor does resumed crawling prove indexing or a ranking improvement. Keep the incident's completion criteria separate from the longer search-performance review. Otherwise a team may reopen a fixed delivery incident because an unrelated commercial metric has not moved.

Compare the evidence before and after the repair

Keep a short before-and-after record for the endpoint, the rules content and the crawler observations. State which observations were available and which were not. If logs are missing for part of the incident, leave that period unknown rather than reconstructing a precise outage from memory.

Check a representative content URL as well. The rules can recover while the page still has its own delivery or indexing problem. Conversely, the page may have stayed available throughout. Reporting those separately makes the scope of the incident clear to content and marketing teams.

If another AI or search crawler appears relevant to the business question, investigate it as a separate provider-specific task. Do not infer its caching or error handling from Googlebot's documented sequence. A shared file format does not establish identical operational behavior across products.

Make the rules endpoint part of release verification

Add the public robots.txt endpoint to the checks you already perform after routing, hosting or gateway changes. Verify its content as well as its status. The useful assertion is that the approved rules remain available at the intended address after a real deployment.

Keep monitoring proportionate to the site. A small business does not need a sprawling crawler dashboard to notice that one important endpoint has stopped working. It needs a clear owner, a repeatable check and an alert that reaches someone able to repair the route.

For the next investigation, start with one question: did the crawler receive the rules you intended to serve? Once that answer is supported, decide whether the remaining problem concerns access, page delivery, indexing or content. That order keeps a small infrastructure failure from turning into a week of unsupported copy changes.
